$comment: Street-name normalisation rules, English — SPEC.md §4.3.
One file per language, in this directory, and the language is the one
the ADDRESS BASE is written in, not the one the interface speaks: an
index built over Antwerp is searched in Dutch whatever the phone is
set to. The index says which file it was built with (§15.1), so the
two can never be paired wrongly.
Read by tools/build_address_index.py AND embedded in the APK, where
the search engine reads it again. A divergence between the two would
make streets unfindable, hence the shared file.
English writes the type AFTER the name — "Baker Street", "Abbey
Road" — so there is next to nothing to split off the head. What
earns its place here is the expansion of the postal abbreviations,
which is what makes "Abbey Rd" and "Abbey Road" the same street.
"st" is deliberately expanded to "saint" at the head only: in
English it is Saint before a name and Street after one, and only
the first position settles it.
This file is also the one any language without rules of its own
falls back on (§9): plain folding, no street type, which still
finds a street typed in full.
Expanded during normalisation, on whole words only. A
single-letter abbreviation is expanded at the head of a name
only, otherwise it would rewrite an initial in the middle of a
person's name.
The street type is stored in a field SEPARATE from the proper
name (§4.3), and is recognised at the HEAD of a name only, by
longest match. Written in their already normalised form.
A language that writes its type last, or glues it to the name,
has few entries here or none at all: that is a fact about the
language, not an omission.

$letterReplacementsComment: Letters that survive accent removal, because they are not accented
letters at all: NFD decomposition has nothing to take off them.
They are folded here instead, on both sides of the search alike.
$punctuationComment: Turned into word breaks on both sides of the search. The
non-breaking spaces are here rather than left to the whitespace
split: Python treats them as whitespace and Kotlin's \s does not,
so a name holding one would be indexed as two words and searched as

$comment: Stop words ignored when RANKING — never when indexing,
otherwise a name would lose half its content. They serve not to
reward a match that only bears on an article.

$referenceNamesComment: Names written out on purpose, replayed by the Kotlin test against
every network generated in this language. They are what proves the
Python script and the application read these rules the same way,
from the day the rules are written rather than from the day a city
of this language has its data generated.
referenceNames: Dr Martin Luther King Jr Blvd
